title: Islam: remembrance
hookLine: in the remembrance of God hearts find rest (Quran 13:28)

lines: TWO IN THE MORNING, MIND RACING.
cards: Two in the morning, and a mind that won't stop. It replays the conversation from lunch, rehearses tomorrow's meeting, lists everything that could go wrong. Push the thoughts away and they come back louder.

A few hours later, across town, an old man sits in a mosque after the dawn prayer, beads slipping through his fingers, lips moving softly, the same few words again and again. He looks rested. Today: dhikr, remembrance.

teach.b: Dhikr means remembrance, and also mention: to remember God, and to say God's name. The Qur'an asks for it often.
From surah thirteen, in Marmaduke Pickthall's 1930 translation: "Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest!" Not by solving everything, but by remembering.
Another verse makes it a two-way street: remember me, God says, and I will remember you.
The simplest dhikr is short phrases: subhanallah, glory be to God; alhamdulillah, praise be to God; Allahu akbar, God is greater.
Hadith reports teach them after the daily prayers, thirty-three times each or close to it, counted on the fingers or on prayer beads called a misbaha or tasbih.

And a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari tells that when Fatima, daughter of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, was worn out from hard work and asked for a servant, he taught her to say these same phrases at bedtime, and said they were better for her than a servant.

teach.h: SILENT OR ALOUD, ALONE OR TOGETHER.
teach.b: Dhikr can be silent or aloud, alone or together. Among Sufis, the mystical tradition within Islam, groups gather to chant God's names in rhythm, and some Sufi orders pair the words with the breath or with movement.

Some keep a quiet dhikr going all day: a phrase at the bus stop, while walking, while falling asleep. The idea is that the heart is always remembering something. Dhikr gives it something that can hold its weight.

how: After the daily prayers Muslims often say subhanallah, alhamdulillah and Allahu akbar on their fingers or prayer beads, and Sufi communities gather for dhikr sessions of chanted remembrance.

o: a prayer said only during Ramadan
remembering God by repeating short phrases
a Friday sermon given at the mosque

s: the Qur'an says hearts find rest in the remembrance of God
dhikr must always be chanted aloud in a group
it can be silent or aloud, alone or together.
a hadith says these phrases were taught to Fatima instead of a servant
the Prophet said they'd be better for her than a servant.

games.q: Fatima is exhausted from hard work and asks her father for a servant. what does he give her?
o: a few phrases to say at bedtime.
games.why: the hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says he taught her subhanallah, alhamdulillah and Allahu akbar to say at bedtime, better for her than a servant.

practice: Choose a word that settles you: if you're Muslim, it might be Allah or alhamdulillah; if not, peace, or here, or thank you. Say it on each out-breath, silently or softly.
When the mind runs off, don't scold it; just come back to the word.

wordCard.voice: Dhikr. Remembrance: short phrases said again and again, so that, as the Qur'an says, hearts find rest. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: hearts find rest. A racing mind can be given one word to hold. Day two hundred sixty-nine, done.

sources.q: Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest!

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 3113 (Fatima, at bedtime); Sahih Muslim 596–597 (after prayer)
